YOu whoreſon drunken ſlaue you had beſt be gone, And empty your drunken panch ſomewhere elſe, For in this houſe thou ſhalt not reſt to night.
speeches.Slie: Tilly vally, by criſee Tapſter Ile feſe you anone, Fills the tother pot, and all's paid for: looke you, I doe drinke it of mine owne inſtigation, Heere Ile lie awhile: why Tapſter I ſay, Fills a freſh cuſhen heere, Heigh ho, heere's good warme lying. Tapſter, giues alittle ſmal ale: Heigh ho. For which Lord? Come Sim, where be the plaiers? Sim ſtand by me, And weele flowt the plaiers out of their coates. Sim, giues ſome more wine, what all the Players gone? am not I a Lord? Who's this? Tapſter, O Lord ſirrha, I haue had the braueſt dreame to night, that euer thou heardeſt in all thy life.
speeches.Lord: Now that the gloomy ſhadow of the night, Longing to view Orions driſling lookes, Leapes from th'antarticke world vnto the skie, And dims the welkin with her pitchie breath, And darkeſome night oreſhades the criſtall heauens, Heere breake we off our hunting for to night. Couple vppe the hounds and let vs 〈…〉 And bid the huntſman lee them 〈…〉 For they haue all deſeru'd it well to daie. But ſoft, what ſleepie fellow is this • res heere? Or is he dead, ſee one what he 〈…〉 Very well ſirha, ſee that they want nothing. How now, what is all things readie? Then ſound the muſicke and Ile wake him ſtrait, And ſee you doe as earſt I gaue in charge. My Lord, my Lord, he ſleepes ſoundly, my Lord. Heere's wine, my Lord, the pureſt of the grape. For your honor, my Lord. My Lord this is but the play, the'yre but in ieſt.
My Lord, tis nothing but a drunken ſleepe His head is too heauie for his bodie, And he hath drunke ſo much that he can go no furder.
Fie, how the ſlauiſh villaine ſtinkes of drinke. Ho, ſirha ariſe. What ſo found aſleepe? Goe take him vp, and beare him to my houſe, And beare him eaſily for feare he wake, And in my faireſt chamber make a fire, And ſet a ſumptuous banquet on the boord, And put my richeſt garments on his backe, Then ſet him at the Table in a chaire: When tha • 〈◊〉 done, againſt he ſhall awake, Let heaue •• y muſicke play about him ſtill, Go two of you away, and beare him hence, And then Ile tell you what I haue deuiſde, But ſee in any caſe you wake him not. Now take my cloke, and giue me one of yours, All fellowes now, and ſee you take me ſo: For we will waite vpon this drunken man, To ſee his countenance when he doth awake, And find himſelfe clothed in ſuch attire, With heauenly muſicke ſounding in his eares, And ſuch a banquet ſet before his eyes, The fellow ſure will thinke he is in heauen, But we will about him when he wakes, And ſee you call him Lord at euery word, And offer thou him his horſe to ride abroad, And thou his hawkes and houndes to hunt the deere ▪ And I will aske what ſutes he meanes to weare, And what ſo ere he ſaith ſee you doo not laugh, But ſtill perſwade him that he is a Lord. The fitteſt time they could haue choſen out, Bid one or two of them come hither ſtraight, Now will I fit my ſelfe accordinglie, For they ſhall play to him when he awakes. Now ſirs, what ſtore of plaies haue you? And whats the name of your Comedie? The taming of a ſhrew, thats excellent ſure, Go ſee that you make you readie ſtraight, For you muſt plaie before a lord to night, Say you are his men and I your fellow, Hee's ſomething fooliſh, but what ſo ere he ſaies, See that you be not daſht out of countenance. And ſirha, go you make you readie ſtraight, And dreſſe your ſelfe like ſome louelie ladie, And when I cal, ſee that you come to me, For I will ſay to him thou art his wife, Dally with him and hug him in thine armes, And if he deſire to got to bed with thee, Then faine ſome ſcuſe and ſay thou wilt anon. Be gone I ſay, and ſee thou dooſt it well. Now ſirs, go you and make you ready too, For you muſt play aſſoone as he doth wake. More richer far your honour hath to weare, And if it pleaſe you I will fetch them ſtraight. Simon and if it pleaſe your honour. I my gracious Lord, and your louely ladie Long time hath mourned for your abſence heere. And now with ioy behold where ſhe dooth come To gratulate your honours ſafe returne. I my Lord. May it pleaſe you, your honors plaiers be come To offer your honour a plaie. I my Lord. Yes my Lord. Euen when it pleaſe your honor, they be readie. Ile cal them my lord. Ho where are you there? Sound Trumpets. Heele come againe my Lord anon. So I do my Lord. My Lord heere comes the Plaiers againe. I my Lord. No more they ſhal not, my Lord, They be runne away. Here my Lord. Who's within there? come hither ſirs, my Lords Aſleepe againe, go take him eaſily vp, And put him in his own apparel againe, And lay him in the place where we did find him, Iuſt vnderneath the alehouſe ſide below, But ſee you wake him not in any caſe.
And it pleaſe your honour your plaiers be come And doo attend your honours pleaſure here.
Mary my lord you may haue a Tragicall, Or acommoditie, or what you will. Marrie my lord tis calde The taming of a Shrew. Tis a good leſſon for vs my L. for vs that are maried men O braue, ſirha Tom, we muſt play before A fooliſh Lord, come lets go make vs ready ▪ Go get a diſhclout to make cleane your ſhooes, And Ile ſpeake for the properties, My Lord, we muſt Haue a ſhoulder of mutton for a propertie, And a little vinegre to make our Diuell rore. I warrant you maſter and you take my councel. I faith ſir, my maſter's going to this geere now Sander, I faith you are a beaſt, I crie God hartilie mercy, my harts ready to run out of my belly with laughing, I ſtood behinde the doore al this while, And heard what you ſaid to hir. You ſpoke like an aſſe to hir, ile tell you what, And I had been there to haue woo'd hir, and had this Cloke that you haue, chud haue had hir before ſhe Had gone a foot furder, and you talke of Woodcoks for al this. With hir, and I cannot tell you what. I mary, twas more by hap then any good cunning, I hope ſheele make you one of the head men of the pariſh ſhortly. I warrant you maiſter, feare not me ▪ For doing of my buſineſſe. Now hang him that has not a liuery cote To ſlaſh it out and ſwaſh it out amongſt the prowdeſt On them. Why looke you now, ile ſcarce put vp Plaine Sander now at any of their hands, for and any Body haue any thing to do with my maſter, ſtraight They come crouching vpon me, I beſeech you good M. Sander ſpeake a good word for me, and then I am ſo Stowt and take it vpon me, and ſtand vpon my pantofles To them out of all crie, why I haue a life like a giant Now, but that my maſter hath ſuch a peſtilent mind To a woman now of late, and I haue a prety wench To my ſiſter, and I had thought to haue preferred my Maſter to hir, and that would haue bin a good Deale in my way, but that hees ſped already. Souns friend, well met. I hold my life he • ee • not my maſters liuery coate, Plaine friend hop of my thum, know you who we are? The ſlaue is ſorie for his fault, now we cannot be angry, well whats the matter that you would do with vs? I and thou beeſt not blind thou maiſt • ee, Ecce ſignum, here. I, it may be, & you tell vs from whence you come. Do you ſerue him, and whats your name? Cake and pie, O my teeth waters to haue a peece of thee. Nay thou muſt firſt tel me where thy maiſter is. For I haue good newes for him, I can tel thee. Marry ſir my maiſter ſends you word That you muſt come to his wedding to morrow. Faith I, you thinke he ſtandes as long about it as you do. Marry hee's gone to our houſe in the Countrey To make al things in a readineſſe againſt my new Miſtriſſe comes thither, but heele come againe to morrow. Boy, oh diſgrace to my perſon! ſounes, boy Of your face, you haue many boyes with ſuch Pickadenaunts I am ſure, ſouns would you Not haue a bloudy noſe for this? The pie? I, you haue more mind of your belly Then to go ſee what your maiſter dooes. Why you may take it, and the diuel burſt You with it, one cannot ſaue a bit after ſupper, But you are alwaies ready to munch it vp. O braue, I would I had eate no meate this weeke, For I haue neuer a corner left in my belly To put a venſon paſtie in, I thinke I ſhall burſt my ſelfe With eating, for ile ſo cram me down the tarts And the marchpanes out of all crie. Let my maſter alone with her for that, for Heele make hir tame wel inongh ere long I warrant thee, For he's ſuch a churle waxen now of late, that and he be Neuer ſo little angry he thums me out of all cry, But in my mind ſirha, the yongeſt is a very Prety wench, and if I thought thy maſter would Not haue hir, Ide haue a fling at hir My ſelfe, ile ſee ſoone whether twill be a match Or no: and it will not, ile ſet the matter Hard for my ſelfe I warrant thee. Oh cruel iudgement, nay then ſirha, My tongue ſhal talke no more to you, marry my Timber ſhal tell the truſty meſſage of his maiſter Euen on the very forehead on thee, thou abuſious Villaine, therefore prepare thy ſelfe. O ſupernodical foole! wel, ile take your Two ſhillings, but ile bar ſtriking at legs. Here take your two ſhillings againe, Ile ſee thee hangd ere ile fight with thee, I gat a broken ſhin the other day, Tis not whole yet, and therefore ile not fight. Come, come, why ſhould we fal out? Which horſe, your c •• all? The Oſtler wil not let me haue him, you owe ten pence For his meate and 6 pence for ſtuffing my miſtris ſaddle. Shal I giue them another pecke of lauender? I pray you maſter lets ſtay til dinner be done. Come ſirs, prouide all things as faſt as you can, For my maiſter's hard at hand, and my new miſtris And all, and he ſent me before to ſee all things ready. Yea and that thou ſhalt find, I can tell thee and if thou doſt not pleaſe her wel: why my maſter haz ſuch ado with her, as it paſſeth, and hee's euen like a mad man. Why Ile tell you what: when they ſhould Goe to church to be married, he puts on an olde Ierkin, and a paire of canuaſſe breeches downe to the Small of his leg, and a red cap on his head, and he Lookes as thou wouldſt burſt thy ſelfe with laughing When thou ſeeſt him: hee's ee'n as good as a Foole for me: and then when they ſhould goe to dinner, He made me ſaddle the horſe, and away he came, And ne'r tarried for dinner, and therefore you had beſt Get ſupper ready againſt they come, for They be hard at hand I am ſure by this time. Now, adſum, ſir. I forſooth. I hurt his foote for the nonce man. Come miſtris. I marry miſtris, but you know my maiſter Has giuen me a charge that you muſt eat nothing, But that which he himſelfe giueth you. You ſay true indeed. Why looke you miſtris, What ſay you to a pece of bieffe and muſtard now? I, I could helpe you to ſome, but that I doubt the muſtard is too chollerick for you. But what ſay you to a ſheepes head and garlicke? I but the garlicke I doubt will make your breath Stincke, and then my maſter wil courſe me for letting You eate it But what ſay you to a fat Capon? Nay berlady then tis too deere for vs, we muſt Not meddle with the Kings meate. Sounes are you ſo light fingred with a murrin, Ile keepe you faſting for it theſe two daies. Here comes my maſter now, heele courſe you. Enter Ferando with a peece of meate vpon his. dagger point and Polidor with him. Yes ſir ile carrie it hence: Maſter let hir Haue none, for ſhe can fight as Hungry as ſhe is. Maſter, the Haberdaſher has brought my Miſtris home hir cap here. Here is the Taylor too with my miſtris gowne. I thats true. That's a lie maiſter, I ſaid two truncke ſleeues. Maiſter if euer I ſaid looſe bodies gowne, Sew me in a ſeame, and beat me to death With a bottome of browne thred. I ſay the note lies in his throate and thou too, And thou ſaiſt it. Dooſt thou heare Tailor, thou haſt braued Many men: braue not me. Th'aſt fac'd many men. Face not me, i'le neither be fac'd nor braued At thy hands I can tell thee. Souns villaine, not for thy life, touch it not: Souns, take vp my miſtris gowne to his Maiſters vſe! I will ſir I warrant you.
Feare not my Lord, Ile handle him well enough And make him thinke I loue him mightilie. Oh that my louelie Lord would once vouchſafe To looke on me, and leaue theſe frantike fits, Or were I now but halfe ſo eloquent, To paint in words what Ile performe in deedes, I know your honour then would pittie me. I warrant you my lord, I will not leaue you thus. I will ſir, and fetch him preſently. Friend, well met. Truſt me ſir it is the vſe where I was borne, To ſalute men after this manner, yet notwithſtanding If you be angry with me for calling of you friend, I am the more ſorry for it, hoping the ſtile Of a Foole wil make you amends for all. Marry ſir, I heare you pertaine to ſeignior Ferando. Shal I intreat you to do me a meſſage to your Maſter? Marrie ſir I ſerue young Polidor your maiſters friend My name ſirha? I tel the ſirha is cald Catapie. Why ſlaue, wouldſt thou eate me? San Eate thee, who would not eate Cake and pie? Why villaine my name is Catapie, But wilt thou tel me where thy maiſter is. Why ſee where he comes. I will ſir: come Saunder. Come hither ſirha, boy. Come, come, I did but ieſt, where is that Same peece of pie that I gaue thee to keepe? Why come man, we ſhall haue good cheere Anon at the bridehouſe, for your maiſter's gone to Church to be married already, and theres Such cheere as paſſeth. I, but how wilt thou do now thy maiſter's Maried, thy miſtres is ſuch a diuel, as ſheele make Thee forget thy eating quickely, ſhee'le beate thee ſo. Come hither thou imperfectious ſlaue, in Regard of thy beggery, hold thee, theres Two ſhillings for thee, to pay for the Healing of thy left leg which I meane Furiouſly to inuade, or to maime at the leaſt. Not I, for ile ſtrike any where. It ſhalbe done my Lord, come help to beare him hence. I wil ſir. She bade mee tell you that ſhee will not come, And you haue any buſineſſe, you muſt come to hir.
So ſirha, now go call my Lord, And tell him that all things are ready as he willd it.
speeches.Another: Set thou ſome wine vpon the boord, And then Ile go fetch my Lord preſently.
Who I, am I a Lord? Ieſus what fine apparell haue I got. By the maſſe I thinke I am a Lord indeed, Whats thy name? Sim, thats as much to ſay Simion or Simon Put forth thy hand and fill the pot. Giue me thy hand, Sim am I a lord indeed? Sim. Is this ſhe? Maſſe tis a prettie wench, whats her name? Harke you miſtreſſe, will you eate a peece of bread? Come ſit downe on my knee, Sim drinke to hir Sim, For ſhe and I will go to bed anon. A plaie Sim, O braue, be they my plaiers? Is there not a foole in the plaie? When will they plaie Sim? Doo, but looke that you come againe. Heere Sim, I drinke to thee. O braue, heers two fine gentlewomen. Sim, muſt they be married now? Looke Sim, the foole is come againe now. I ſay weele haue no •• nding to priſon. I tel thee Sim weele haue no ſending, To priſon thats flat: why Sim, am not I Don Chriſto Vari? Therefore I ſay, they ſhal not goe to priſon. Are they run away Sim? thats wel, Then gis ſome more drinke, and let them play againe. drinkes and then fals aſleepe. Wil ſhe? I know now how to tame a ſhrew, I dreamt vpon it all this night till now, And thou haſt wakt me out of the beſt dreame That euer I had in my life: but Ile to my wife preſently, and tame her too if ſhe anger me.
And if your honour pleaſe to ride abroad, Ile fetch your luſtie ſteedes more ſwift of pace Then winged Pegaſus in all his pride, That ran ſo ſwiftlie ouer Perſian plaines. Why Sander, what doth he ſay? Forſooth Iohn Cooke. I laft what a boxe he gaue Sander For pulling off his bootes.
And if your honour pleaſe to hunt the deere, Your hounds ſtands readie cuppled at the doore, Who in running will oretake the Row, And make the long breathde Tygre broken winded. Welcome home Sander: ſirrha how lookes our new miſtris, they ſay ſhee's a plaguy ſhrew? Sowns, ſee where they be already. Sownes, I thinke of my conſcience my maiſter's madde ſince he was married.
speeches.Boy: My Lord, Ile go bid them begin their plaie. Tuſh, tis no matter man, I prethee giue it me, I am very hungry I promiſe thee. Souns you ſlaue, wil you be a Riuall with My maſter in his loue? ſpeake but ſuch Another word and ile cut off one of thy legs.
Welcome to Athens my beloued friend, To Platoes ſchoole and Ariſtotles walks, Welcome from Ceſtus famous for the loue Of good Leander and his Tragedie, For whome the Heleſpont weepes briniſh teares, The greateſt griefe is I cannot as I would Giue entertainment to my deereſt friend. Why how now my Lord, what, in adumpe, To ſee theſe damſels paſſe away ſo ſoone? I cannot blame your honor, good my Lorde, For they are both louely, wiſe, faire, and yong, And one of them, the yongeſt of the three I long haue lou'd (ſweet frind) and ſhe lou'd me, But neuer yet we could not find a meanes How we might compaſſe our deſired ioyes. Yes truſt me, but he hath ſolemnly ſworne, His eldeſt daughter firſt ſhall be eſpowſde, Before he grants his yongeſt leaue to loue: And therefore he that meanes to get their loues ▪ Muſt firſt provide for her, if he wil ſpeed, And he that hath her ſhall be fretted ſo, As good be wedded to the diuell himſelfe, For ſuch a skould as ſhe did neuer liue, And til that ſhe be ſped, none elſe can ſpeede: Which makes me thinke, that all my labors loſt, And who ſoere can get hir firme good will, A large dowrie he ſhall be ſure to haue, For hir father is a man of mightie wealth, And an antient Citizen of the towne, And that was he that went along with them. I like your choiſe, and glad you choſe not mine, Then if you like to follow on your loue, We muſt deuiſe a meanes to find ſome one That will attempt to wed this deuiliſh skould, And I do know the man. Come hither boy, Go your waies ſirha, to Ferandoes houſe, Deſire him to take the paines to come to me, For I muſt ſpeake with him immediatly. A man I thinke will fit hir humour right, As blunt in ſpeech as ſhe is ſharpe in tongue, And he I thinke will match hir euery way, And yet he is a man of wealth ſufficient, And for his perſon worth as good as ſhe: And if he compaſſe hir to be his wife, Then may we freely viſit both our loues. Here comes them an that I did tel you of. I would thy •• ſter once were in the vaine, To trie himſelfe how he could woo a wench. Whither in faith Ferando? tel me true. How like you this Aurelius, I thinke he knew Our minds before we ſent to him, But tell me, when do ye meane to ſpeake with hir? With all my heart, come Aurelius, Let vs be gone and leaue him here alone. Come ſweet Aurelius my faithfull friend, Now wil we go to ſee thoſe louely dames, Richer in beauty then the orient pearle, Whiter than is the Alpine Chriſtall mould, And far more louely than the terrene plant, That bluſhing in the aire turnes to a ſtone. What Sander, what newes with you? What, ſhal he be married then? Whither is thy maiſter gone now? This is ſuddainly diſpatcht belike: Wel, ſirha boy, take Sander in with you, And haue him to the buttrey preſentlie. I Valeria, for he ſpoke to me, To helpe him to ſome cunning Muſition, To teach his eldeſt daughter on the lute, And thou I know wilt fitte his turne ſo well, As thou ſhalt get great fauour at his hands, Be gone Valeria, and ſay I ſent thee to him. Now ſweet Aurelius, by this deuiſe Shal we haue leiſure for to court our loues, For whilſt that ſhe is learning on the lute, Hir ſiſters may take time to ſteale abrode, For otherwiſe ſheele keepe them both within. And make them worke whilſt ſhe herſelfe doth play. But come, lets go vnto Alfonſos houſe, And ſee how Valeria and Kate agrees I doubt his muſicke ſcarce will pleaſe his skoller, But ſtay, heere comes Alfonſo. He is, I pray you ſir bid him welcome, He's a wealthy Marchants ſon of Ceſtus. Such newes I heard, and I came now to know. Come then Aurelius, come in with me, And weele go ſit a while and chat with them, And after bring them forth to take the aire. His Tailor, it may be, hath bin too ſlacke In his apparrell which he meanes to weare: For no queſtion but ſome fantaſtike ſutes He is determined to weare to day, And richly powdered with pretious ſtones, Spotted with liquide golde, thicke ſet with pearle, And ſuch he meanes ſhall be his wedding ſutes. Fie Ferando, not thus attired for ſhame, Come to my Chamber, and there 〈◊〉 thy ſelfe, Of twenty ſutes that I did neuer weare. Farewell Ferando, ſince you will be gone. I pray you ſir let it ſtand, for ile eate Some with her my ſelfe. Come faire Emelia, the prieſt is gon, And at the church your father and the reſt Do ſtay to ſee our marriage rites perform'd, And knit in ſight of heauen this Gordian knot, That teeth of fretting Time may ne'r vntwiſt, Then come faire loue and gratulate with me This daies content and ſweet ſolemnity. No maruel of Ferando be away, His wife I thinke hath troubled ſo his wits, That he remaines at home to keepe them warme, For forward wedlocke as the prouerbe ſayes, Hath brought him to his nightcap long ago. And good my Lord, let vs intreat your grace To purge your ſtomacke of this Melancoly, Taint not your princely mind with griefe my Lord, But pardon and forgiue theſe louers faults, That kneeling craue your gratious fauor here. Nay then Ferando he muſt needes ſit out, For he may cal I thinke til he be weary, Before his wife wil come before ſhe liſt. I take it. Ile lay as much to yours, That my wife comes as ſoone as I do ſend. I, were it a thouſand pounds I durſt preſume On my wiues loue: and I wil lay with thee. And ſo wil I vpon my faith I vow. Now, wher's your miſtris? Wel ſir, I pray you lets heare what Anſwere your wife will make. Oh wonderful metamorphoſis. But thou Emelia haſt loſt me a great deale more. Well, ſince tis done, come, lets goe.
Thankes noble Polidor my ſecond ſelfe, The faithfull loue which I haue found in thee Hath made me leaue my fathers princelie court, The Duke of Ceſtus thriſe renowmed ſeate, To come to Athens thus to find thee out, Which, ſince I haue ſo happily attaind, My fortune now I do account as great As earſt did Caeſar when he conquered moſt, But tel me noble friend, where ſhal we lodge, For I am vnacquainted in this place. With all my heart, I wil requite thy loue. But ſtaie; what dames are theſe ſo bright of hew Whoſe eies are brighter than the lampes of heauen? Fairer then rocks of pearle and pretious ſtone, More louely far then is the morning ſunne, When firſt ſhe opes hir oriental gates. Truſt me my friend I muſt confeſſe to thee, I tooke ſo much delight in theſe faire dames As I do wiſh they had not gone ſo ſoone: But if thou canſt, reſolue me what they be, And what old man it was that went with them, For I do long to ſee them once againe. Why, is not her father willing to the match? But he ſhall keepe hir ſtil by my aduiſe, And yet I needes muſt loue his ſecond daughter The image of honor and nobility, In whoſe ſweet perſon is compriſde the ſumme Of Natures skill and heauenly maieſty. O might I ſee the cenſer of my loule Whoſe ſacred beauty hath inchanted me, More faire then was the Grecian Helena For whoſe ſweet ſake ſo many princes dide; That came with thouſand ſhips to Tenedos. But when we come vnto hir fathers houſe, Tel him I am a Merchants ſonne of Ceſtus, That comes for trafficke vnto Athens here, And here ſirha, I wil change with you for once, And now be thou the Duke of Ceſtus ſonne, Reuel and ſpend as if thou wert my felfe, For I will court thy loue in this diſguiſe. Tuſh feare not Valeria, let me alone, But ſtay, here comes ſome other company. Valeria, as erſt wee did deuiſe, Take thou thy lute and go to Alfonſos houſe, And ſay that Polidor ſent thee thither. I thanke you ſir, and if what I haue got By marchandiſe or trauel on the ſeas, Sattins, or lawnes, or azure coloured ſilke, Or pretious fiery pointed ſtones of Indy, You ſhall command, both them, my ſelf, and all. Why Valeria, will ſhe not learne apace? Faith he's gon vnto the taming ſchoole. I: and Ferando is the maiſter of the ſchoole. Faith I know not: but by ſome odde deuiſe Or other, but come Valeria I long to ſee the man, By whom we muſt compriſe our plotted drift, That I may tel him what we haue to do. Agreede then, lets go. Now Seignior Phylotus, we wil go Vnto Alfonſos houſe, and be ſure you ſay As I did tel you, concerning the man That dwels at Ceſtus, whoſe ſon I ſaid I was, For you do very much reſemble him, And feare not: you may be bold to ſpeake your mind. Thanks ſweet Phylotus, then ſtay you here, And I will go and fetch him hither ſtrait. Ho, Seignior Alfonſo: a word with you. My father ſir is newly come to towne, And I haue brought him here to ſpeake with you, Concerning theſe matters that I told you of, And he can certifie you of the truth. He is the Duke of Ceſtus thriſe renowmed ſon, Who for the loue his honor beares to me, Hath thus accompanied mee to this place. Sweet Phylema bewties minerall, From whence the ſun exhales his glorious ſhine, And clad the heauen in thy reflected raies, And now my liefeſt loue, the time drawes nie, That Himen mounted in his ſaffron robe, Muſt with his torches waite vpon thy traine, As Hellens brothers on the horned moone. Now Iuno to thy number ſhal I adde, The faireſt bride that euer marchant had. Pardon me father, humbly on my knees I do intreat your grace to heare me ſpeake. Then let my death ſweet father end your griefe, For I it is that thus haue wrought your woes, Then be reuengd on me, for here I ſweare That they are innocent of what I did, Oh had I charge to cut off Hydraes head, To make the to pleſſe Alpes a champaine field, To kil vntamed monſters with my ſword, To trauel daily in the hotteſt ſun, And watch in winter when the nights be cold. I would with gladnes vndertake them all, And thinke the paine but pleaſure that I felt, So that my noble father at my return, Would but forget and pardon me my offence. Not yet my Lord, ile bring you to your ſhip. Faith if you wil, in trial of our wiues Who wil come ſooneſt at their husbands cal. My wife comes ſooneſt for a hundred pound. How now Ferando, you dare not lay belike. Faith father a waighty cauſe, about our wiues, Fiue hundred markes already we haue laid, And he whoſe wife doth ſhew moſt loue to him, He muſt inioy the wager to himſelfe. Ile ſend for my wife firſt, Valeria, Go bid your miſtris come to me. Now for my hundred pound, Would any lay ten hundred more with me I know I ſhould obtaine it by her loue. Truſt me Ferando I am ſure you haue, For you I dare preſume haue loſt it al. Now ſir ha, what ſaies your miſtris? I thinke my wife for all ſhe did not come, Wil proue moſt kind, for now I haue no feare, For I am ſure Ferandos wife, ſhe will not come. This is a wonder, almoſt paſt beleefe. Beſhrew thee Phylema thou haſt Loſt me a hundred pound to night, For I did lay that thou wouldſt firſt haue come. Beleeue me father, I rejoyce to ſee Ferando and his wife ſo louingly agree.
My Lord, if you vouchſafe of ſchollers fare, My houſe, my ſelfe, and al is yours to vſe, You and your men ſhall ſtaie and lodge with me. Agreed, Boy deſire your miſtris to come hither.
Daughters, be gone, and hie you to the church, And I will hie me downe vnto the key To ſee what marchandiſe is come aſhore. Seignior Ferando y'are welcome hartily, You are a ſtranger ſir vnto my houſe, Harke you ſir, looke what I did promiſe you Ile performe, if you get my daughters loue. Ha Kate, Come hither wench and liſt to me, Vſe this gentleman friendly as thou canſt. How now Feranda, what, my daughter? Come hither Kate, and let me giue thy hand To him that I haue choſen for thy loue, And thou to morrow ſhalt be wed to him. Giue me thy hand, Ferando loues thee well, And will with wealth and eaſe maintaine thy ſtate. Here Ferando, take her for thy wiſe. And ſunday next ſhall be our wedding day. Do ſo, come Kate, why doſt thou looke So ſad? be mery wench, thy wedding daie's at hand, Sonne, fare you wel, and ſee you keepe your promiſe What M. Polidor! you are wel met, I thanke you for the man you ſent to me, A good Muſition I thinke he is; I haue ſet my daughter and him togither, But is this gentleman a friend of yours? Y'are welcome ſir, and if my houſe afforde You any thing that may content your mind, I pray you ſir make bold with me. Thanks gentle ſir, Polidor take him in, And bid him welcome vnto my houſe, For thou I thinke muſt be my ſecond ſonne; Ferando, Polidor dooſt thou not know Muſt marry Kate, and to morrow is the day. Polidor tis true, go let me alone, For I muſt ſee againſt the bridegroome come, That al things be according to his mind, And ſo ile leaue you for an houre or two. I car'd not I, what coſt he did beſtow, In golde, or ſilke, ſo he himſelfe were here, For I had rather loſe a thouſand crownes, Than that he ſhould deceiue vs heere to day: But ſoft, I thinke I ſee him come. Yea mary ſonne, we were almoſt perſwaded, That we ſhould ſcarce haue had our Bridegroome heere: But ſay, why art thou thus baſely attired? I prethee Ferando let me intreat Before thou go'ſt vnto the church with vs, To put ſome other ſute vpon thy backe. Come gentlemen go along with vs, For thus, do what we can, he will be wed. Your horſe! what ſon, I hope you do but ieſt, I am ſure you wil • o • go ſo ſuddainely. Why ſon, I hope at leaſt youle dine with vs. So mad a couple did I neuer ſee. God hold it, that it may continue ſtill, I would be loath that they ſhould diſagree, But he (I hope) will hold her in a while. Enough Aurelius: but we forget Our marriage dinner now the Bride is gone, Come, let vs ſee what there they left behind. is this your father? you are welcome ſir. Truſt me, I muſt commend your liberal mind, And louing care you beare vnto your ſon, And here I giue him freely my conſent. As for my daughter, I thinke he knowes her mind, And I will inlarge her dowry for your ſake, And ſolemniſe with ioy your nuptial rites. But is this gentleman of Ceſtus too? You were too blame you tolde me not before, Pardon me my Lord, for if I had knowne Your honor had bin here in place with me, I would haue don my duty to your honor. Come louely ſonnes, your marriage rites Performed, Lets hie vs home to ſee what cheere we haue, I wonder that Ferando and his wife Come not to ſee this great ſolemnity. I did not thinke you would preſume, To match your daughter with my princely houſe, And ne'r make mee acquainted with the cauſe. How now ſons, what in conference ſo hard, May I without offence, know where about? Why then Ferando he is ſure to loſe it, I promiſe thee ſon, thy wife wil hardly come, And therefore I would not wiſh thee lay ſo much. Polidor, I dare preſume for thee, I thinke thy wife wil not denie to come, And I do maruel much Aurelius, That your wife came not when you ſent for her. Now Aurelius, what ſay you to this?
My Lord, how if the Duke your father ſhould By ſome meanes come to Athens for to ſee How you do profit in theſe publike ſchooles, And find me clothed thus in your attire, How would he take it then thinke you my Lord? I would, ſweete Miſtris, that it lay in me, To helpe you to that thing that's your delight. If that (ſweet Miſtris) were your harts content, You ſhould commaund a greater thing than that, Although it were ten times to my diſgrace. Why Miſtris, doe you mocke me? Well, will you play alittle? That ſtop was falſe, play it againe. What, doe you bid me kiſſe your arſe? Hold Miſtris, ſowns will you breake my Lute? Sowns, teach her to play on the Lute? The diuell ſhall teach her firſt, I am glad ſhee's gone, For I was ne're ſo fraid in all my life, But that my Lute ſhould flie about mine eares: My maiſter ſhall teach her himſelfe for me, For Ile keepe me farre enough without her reach, For he and Polidor ſent me before, To be with her, and teach her on the Lute, Whilſt they did court the other gentle women, And heere me thinkes they come together. Hee ſaies ſo. The taming ſchoole! why is there ſuch a place? That's rare: but what decorum doth he vſe? Then come my Lord and I will bring you to him ſtraight. Thanks good Alfonſo. but I did come to ſee When theſe marriage rites ſhould be performed. And if in theſe nuptials you vouchſafe, To honor thus the prince of Ceſtus friend, In celebration of his ſpouſal rites, He ſhal remaine a laſting friend to you, What ſaies Aurelius father? Come then Aurelius I wil go with you. Sounes it is the Duke, what ſhall I do? Diſhonor thee? why knowſt thou what thou ſaiſt? I wil my Lord. She is ſomthing buſie but ſheele come anone.
Good morrow gentleman to al at once. How now Polidor, what man ſtill in loue? Euer wooing and canſt thou neuer ſpeed? God ſend me better lucke when I ſhal woo. Why ſirha, are you ſo cunning? Faith I am euen now a going. Faith preſently, do you but ſtand aſide, And I will make hir father bring hir hither: And ſhe, and I, and he, will talke alone. Ho Seignior Alfonſo, who's within there? Then when I haue talke a word or two with hir, Do you ſtep in and giue her hand to me, And tell hir when the mariage day ſhall be, For I do know ſhe would be maried faine, And When our nuptiall rites be once performde Let me alone to tame hir well inough, Now •• ll her forth that I may ſpeake with hir. Twenty good morrows to my louely Kate. I tel thee Kate I know thou lou'ſt me wel. My mind ſweet Kate doth ſay I am the man, Muſt wed, and bed, and marrie bonnie Kate. I, to ſtand ſo long and neuer get a kiſſe. I prithy do Kate, they ſay thou art a ſhrew. And I like thee the better, for I would haue thee ſo. No Kate, this hand is mine, and I thy loue. But yet his bil will ſerue, if the other faile, Shee's willing ſir, and loues me as hir life. Why ſo, did I not tel thee I ſhould be the man? Father, I leaue my louely Kate with you, Prouide your ſelues againſt our mariage day, For I muſt hie me to my country houſe In haſte, to ſee prouiſion may be made, To entertaine my Kate when ſhe doth come. So, al thus far goes well. Ho Sander. Why, dooſt thou thinke that I did not ſpeake wel to hir? Well ſirha, and yet thou ſeeſt I haue got hir Wel ſirha, leaue your ieaſting and go to Polidors houſe, The yong gentleman that was here with me, And tel him the circumſtance of al thou knowſt, Tel him on ſunday next we muſt be married, And if he aske thee whither I am gone, Tel him into the countrey to my houſe, And vpon Sunday ile be here againe. Good morrow father: Polidor well met, You wonder, I know, that I haue ſtaide ſo long. Thus richly father you ſhould haue ſaide, For when my wife and I are married once, Shee's ſuch a ſhrew, if we ſhould once fall out, Sheele pull my coſtly ſutes ouer mine eares, And therefore am I thus attir'd a while: For many things I tell you's in my head, And none muſt know thereof, but Kate and I: For we ſhall liue like Lambes and Lions ſure, Nor Lambs to Lions neuer were ſo tame, If once they be within the Lions pawes, As Kate to me, if we were married once, And therefore, come, le •• to church preſently. Tuſh Polidor, I haue as many ſutes Fantaſtike made to fit my humor ſo, As any in Athens, and as richly wrought As was the Maſsie Robe that late adorn'd The ſtately legat of the Perſian King, And this from them haue I made choiſe to weare. Not for the world, if I might gaine it ſo, And therefore take me thus, or not at al. But ſoft, ſee where my Kate doth come, I muſt ſalute hir: how fares my louely Kate, What, art thou ready? ſhal we go to church? Tuſh Kate theſe words adde greater loue in me, And makes me thinke thee fairer then before: Sweet Kate, thou louelier then Dianas purple to be, Whiter then are the ſnowie Apenis, Or icie haire that growes on Boreas chin. Father, I ſweare by Ibis golden beale, More faire and Radiant is my bony Kate, Then ſiluer Zanthus when he doth imbrace The ruddie Simies at Id • s feete, And care not thou, ſweet Kate, how I be clad, Thou ſhalt haue garments wrought of Median 〈◊〉 , Enchac'd with pretious iewels fetcht from far, By Italian marchants that with Ruſsian ſtemes, Plowes vp huge furrowes in the 〈◊〉 Mai • e, And better far my louely Kate ſhal weare: Then come ſweet loue, and let vs to the church, For this I ſweare ſhal be my wedding ſute. Father farewel, my Kate and I muſt home, Sirha, go make ready my horſe preſently. Tut Kate I tel thee we muſt needes go home, Vilaine, haſt thou ſadled my horſe? Souns you flaue, ſtand you prating here? Saddle the bay gelding for your miſtris. Here villaine, goe pay him ſtrait. Now welcome Kate. Where's theſe villaines Heere? what, not ſupper yet vpon the boord? Nor table ſpread, nor nothing done at all, Where's that villaine that I ſent before? Come hither you villaine, Ile cut your noſe, You rogue, help me off with my bootes: wil't pleaſe You to lay the cloth? Sowns the villaine Hurts my foote: pull eaſily I ſay, yet againe? Sowns, burnt and ſcorch't, who dreſt this meate? Goe you villaines, bring me ſuch meate? Out of my ſight I ſay, and beare it hence: Come Kate, wee'l haue other meate prouided, Is there a fire in my chamber ſir? Did you ſo, you damned villaine? This humour muſt I holde me to a while, To bridle and hold backe my head ſtrong wife, With curbes of hunger, eaſe, and want of ſleepe: Nor ſleepe, nor meate ſhall ſhe enjoy to night, Ile mew her vp as men doe mew their Hawkes, And make her gently come vnto the Lewre, Were ſhe as ſtubborne, or as full of ſtrength, As was the Thracian Horſe Alcides tamde, That king Egeus fed with fleſh of men, Yet would I pull her downe, and make her come, As hungry Hawkes doe flie vnto their Lewre. See heere Kate, I haue prouided meat for thee, Here take it: what, iſt not worthy thanks? Go ſirha, take it away againe, you ſhall be Thankful for the next you haue. Nay now tis not worth a pin, go ſirha and take it hence I ſay. Wel ſirha, ſet it downe againe. I, when ya're meeke and gentle, but not Before, I know your ſtomacke is not yet come downe. Therefore, no maruel thou canſt not eat, And I will go vnto your Fathers houſe, Come Polidor let vs go in againe, And Kate come in with vs, I know ere long, That thou and I ſhall louingly agree. Who ſpoke for it? didſt thou Kate? O monſtrous: why it becomes thee not, Let me ſee it Kate: here ſirha take it hence, This cap is out of faſhion quite. Why true, he meanes to make a foole of thee, To haue thee put on ſuch a curtald cap: Sirha, be gone with it. Let me ſee it Taylor: what, with cuts and jags? Sounes thou vilaine, thou haſt ſpoil'd the gowne. Come hither ſirha: Taylor read the note. Wel ſir, go forward. Go I ſay, and take it vp for your maiſters vſe. Sirha, go fetch our horſes forth, and bring Them to the backe gate preſently. Come Kate, the moone ſhines cleere to night, me thinkes. Yet againe, come backe againe, it ſhal be The moone ere we come at your fathers. Ieſus, ſaueth glorious moone. I am glad Kate your ſtomacke is come downe, I know it well thou knowſt it is the ſun, But I did trie to ſee if thou wouldſt ſpeake, And croſſe me now as thou haſt done before, And truſt me Kate hadſt thou not namde the moone, We had gone backe againe as ſure as death. But ſoft, who's this thats comming here? Why ſo, Kate, this was friendly done of thee, And kindly too ▪ why thus muſt we two liue, One minde, one heart, and one content for both, This good old man dos thinke that we are mad, And glad is he I am ſure, that he is gone, But come ſweet Kate, for we will after him, And now perſwade him to his ſhape againe. Come Gentlemen, nowe that ſupper's done, How ſhall we ſpend the time til we go to bed? Tis wel for you that haue ſuch gentle wiues, Yet in this trial wil I not ſit out, It may be Kate wil come as ſoone as I do ſend. Why true, I dare not lay indeed: But how, ſo little mony on ſo ſure a thing, A hundred pound: why I haue laid as much Vpon my Dog, in running at a Deere, She ſhal not come ſo far for ſuch a trifle, But wil you lay fiue hundred markes with me, And whoſe wife ſooneſt comes when he doth cal, And ſhewes her ſelfe moſt louing vnto him, Let him inioy the wager I haue laid, Now what ſay you? dare you aduenture thus? Tuſh father, were it ten times more I durſt aduenture on my louely Kate, But if I loſe ile pay, and ſo ſhal you. Then ſit we downe and let vs ſend for them: Why ſo, did not I tel you this before, She was buſie and cannot come. I, ſo, ſo, he deſires hir to come. O monſtrous intollerable preſumption, Worſe then a blaſing ſtar, or ſnow at Midſummer, Earthquakes, or any thing vnſeaſonable, She will not come: but he muſt come to hir. ſirha, command your miſtris to come To me preſently. The more's the pitty, then I muſt loſe. But I haue won, for ſee where Kate doth come. I did my loue, I ſent for thee to come, Come hither Kate, whats that vpon thy head? Pul it off and tread it vnder thy feet, Tis fooliſh, I wil not haue thee weare it. She takes off her cap and treads on it. This is a token of her true loue to 〈◊〉 And yet Ile try her further you ſhall ſee, Come hither Kate, where are thy ſiſters? Fetch them hither, and if they wil not come, Bring them perforce and make them come with thee. But you ſhal ſee ſhe wil do more then this, For ſee where ſhe brings her ſiſters forth by force. Tis wel done Kate. Now louely Kate, before their husbands here, I prethee tel vnto theſe head-ſtrong women, What dewty wiues do owe vnto their Husbands. Inough ſweet, the wager thou haſt won, And they I am ſure cannot deny the ſame. Thanks, ſweet father, gentlemen, good night, For Kate and I will leaue you for to night, Tis Kate and I am wed, and you are ſped: And ſo farewell, for we will to our beds.
speeches.San: Who I twere better for you by ſiue ma • e And you could tel how to do it as wel os I.
To bonie Kate, the patientſt wench aliue, The Diuel himſelfe dares ſcarce venture to woo her, Seignior Alfonſos eldeſt daughter, And he hath promiſde me ſix thouſand crownes If I can win her once to be my wife, And ſhe and I muſt woo with skoulding ſure, And I will hold hir too't til ſhe be wearie, Or elſe ile make her yeeld to grant me loue. Out ſlaue, and bring them preſently to the dore. Souns vilaine, art thou here yet? Come Kate, our dinner is prouided at home. I Kate ſo thou ſhalt, but at ſome other time, Whenas thy ſiſters here ſhall be eſpouſd, Then thou and I wil keepe our wedding day, In better ſort then now we can prouide, For heere I promiſe thee before them all, We will ere long returne to them againe: Come Kate, ſtand not on termes, we will away, This is my day, to morrow thou ſhalt rule, And I will doe what euer thou commandes. Gentlemen, farewell, wee'l take our leaues, It will be late before that we come home. I pray God you haue not laid too much already. Wel, wel: Polidor, ſend you for your wife.
You jeaſt I am ſure, is ſhe yours already? The Diuel you do, who told you ſo? Was euer ſeene ſo groſſe an aſſe as this. Hands off I ſay, and get you from this place; Or I will ſet my ten commandements in your face. Let go my hand, for feare it reach your eare. Y faith ſir no, the woodcoke wants his taile. Tis for your skin then, but not to be your wife. Why father, what do you mean to do with me, To giue me thus vnto this brainſicke man, That in his mood cares not to murder me? But yet I will conſent and marry him, (For I me thinkes haue liu'de too long a maide,) And match him too, or elſe his manhood a good. Not for me, for I wil not go. But not for me, for here I meane to dine: Ile haue my wil in this as wel as you, Though you in madding mood would leaue your frinds, Deſpite of you ile tarry with them ſtill. Sander I prethee helpe me to ſome meat, I am ſo faint that I can ſcarcely ſtand. Why man, thy maſter needs neuer know it. Why I ſay tis excellent meat, canſt thou helpe me to ſome? Why any thing, I care not what it be That's meat for a king, ſweete Sander help me to ſome of it. Our villaine, doſt thou mocke me, Take that for thy ſawſineſſe. I tel thee villaine, ile teare the fleſh off Thy face and eate it, and thou prate to me thus. Nay nay I pray you let him take it hence, And keepe it for your owne diet, for ile none, Ile ne're be beholding to you for your meat, I tel thee flatly here vnto thy teeth, Thou ſhalt not keepe me nor feed me as thou liſt, For I will home againe vnto my fathers houſe. The faſhion is good inough: belike you Meane to make a foole of me. The moone? why husband you are deceiu'd, It is the ſun. Why ile ſay as you ſay, it is the moone. Ieſus, ſaue the glorious moone. Faire louely lady, bright and Chriſtaline, Bewteous and ſtately as the eie-traind bird, As glorious as the morning waſht with dew, Within whoſe eies ſhe takes her dawning beames, And golden ſommer ſleepes vpon thy cheekes, Wrapt vp thy radiations in ſome cloud, Leſt that thy bewty make this ſtately towne Inhabitable like the burning Zone, With ſweet reflections of thy louely face. Nothing husband but my cap I thinke. They be ſitting in the bridal chamber. I will. See husband, I haue brought them both. Then you that liue thus by your pampered wils, Now liſt to me, and marke what I ſhal ſay, Th'eternal power that with his only breath, Shall cauſe this end, and this beginning frame, Not in time, nor before time, but with time confus'd, For al the courſe of yeares, of ages, months, Of ſeaſons temperate, of dayes and houres, Are tun'd and ſtopt by meaſure of his hand, The firſt world was, a forme without a forme, A heape confus'd, a mixture al deform'd, A gulfe of gulfes, a body bodileſſe. Where al the elements were orderleſſe, Before the great Commander of the world. The King of kings, the glorious God of heauen, Who in ſix daies did frame his heauenly worke, And made al things to ſtand in perfect courſe, Then to his image he did make a man Olde Adam, and from his ſide aſleepe A rib was 〈◊〉 , of which the Lord did make The woe of man ſo termd by Adam then, Woman, for that by her 〈◊〉 ſinne to vs, And for her ſinne was Adam doom • to die. As Sara to her husband ſo ſhould we, Obey them, loue them, keepe and nouriſh them, If they by any meanes do want our helpes, Laying our hands vnder their feet to tread, If that by that we might procure their eaſe, And for a preſident Ile firſt begin; And lay my hand vnder my husbands feet. She laies her hand vnder her husbands feet.
I will ſir, and ſtay your comming at Alfonſos houſe.
Sim, when will the foole come againe?
Gis ſome more drinke here, ſouns where's The Tapſter, here Sim, eate ſome of theſe things.
The ſenceleſſe trees by muſick haue bin mou'd, And at the ſound of pleſant tuned ſtrings, Haue ſauage beaſts hung downe their liſtning heads, As though they had beene caſt into a traunce. Then it may be, that ſhe to whome naught can pleaſe, With Muſickes ſound, in time may be ſurpriſde. Come louely Miſtris, will you take your lute, And play the leſſon that I taught you laſt? And for to honor him and his faire bride. Ile yeerely ſend you from your fathers court, Cheſts of refind ſugar ſeuerally, Ten tun of tunis wine, ſucket, ſweet drugs, To celebrate and ſolemnize this day, And cuſtom-free, your marchants ſhal commerce And interchange the profits of your land, Sending you gold for braſſe, ſiluer for lead, Caſſes of ſilke for packes of wol and cloth, To bind this friendſhip and confirme this league.
speeches.Kate: It is no matter whether I doe, or no, For truſt me, I take no great delight in it. In you with a peſtlence, are you ſo kind? Then make a night-cap of your fiddles caſe, To warme your head, and hide your filthy face. Y'are ſo kind t'were pittie you ſhould be hang'd, And yet me thinkes the foole doth looke aſquint. No, but I meane to mooue thee. Yea, giue me the Lute. Then mend it thou, thou filthy aſſe. How now jacke ſawce? y'are a jolly mate, Y'are beſt be ſtill leſt I croſſe your pate, And make your muſicke flie about your cares ▪ Ile make it and your coxcombe meet. Yea on thy head and if thou ſpeake to me, There, take it vp, and fi • dle ſomewhere elſe, And ſee you come no more into this place, Leſt that I clap your fiddle on your face. Not I with one ſo mad, ſo baſely tir'd, To marry ſuch a filthy ſlauiſh groome, That as it ſeemes ſometimes is from hi • wits, Or el • e he would not thus haue come to vs. Let him go or tarry, I am reſolu'd to ſtay. And not to trauel on my wedding day. Why I thanke you for it. What if I did? come hither ſirha, giue me The cap, ile ſee if it wil fit me. Come, come, I like the faſhion of it wel inough, Heere's more adoe than needes, I'le haue it, I, And if you doe not like it, hide your eies, I thinke I ſhall haue nothing by your will. Nine aclocke, why tis already paſt two In the afternoone by al the clockes in the towne. I ſay tis two aclocke in the afternoone. Sweete husband did you ſend for me.
speeches.Pol:: How now Valeria, where's your Miſtris? Come faire Emelia, my louely loue, Brighter than the burniſht pallace of the Sunne, The eie- • ight of the glorious firmament, In whoſe bright lookes ſparkles the radiant fire. Wilie Prometheus ſlily ſtole from Ioue, Infuſing breath, life, motion, ſoul • , To euerie object ſtricken by thine eies. Oh faire Emelia, I pine for thee, And, either muſt enjoy thy loue, or die. Thankes faire Emelia for theſe ſweet words: But what ſaith Philena to her friend? Aurelius, or elſe I miſſe my marke: Her tongue will walke, if ſhe doe holde her hands. I am in doubt ere halfe a month be paſt Hee'l curſe the Prieſt that married him ſo ſoone, And yet it may be ſhe will be reclaimde, For ſhe is very patient growne of late. Within theſe two daies I will ride to him, And ſee how louingly they do agree. And ſo to me whilſt Polidor doth liue. Faire Emelia, ſummers bright ſun Queene, Brighter of hew than is the burning clime, Where Phoebus in his bright Aequator ſits, Creating golde and pretious mineralls, What would Emelia doe if I were forc'd To leaue faire Athens, and to range the world?
speeches.Val:: At the vengeance, I thinke, and no where elſe. Yes berladie, ſhe haz learn'd too much alreadie, And that I had felt, had I not ſpoke her faire, But ſhe •• all ne're be learnt for me againe. Feare not my Lord, Ile fetch him ſtrait to you, For hee'l doe any thing that you commaund, But tell me, my Lord, is Ferando married then?
speeches.Aurel:: Well Valeria go to my chamber, And beare him companie that came to daie From Ceſtus, where our aged father dwelles. Miſtris, you ſhall not neede to buy of me: For when I croſs'd the bubbling Canibey, And ſailde along the criſtall Helliſpont, I fill'd my coffers of the wealthy mines, Where I did cauſe millions of labouring Moores To vndermine the cauerns of the earth, To ſeeke for ſtrange and new found pretious ſtones, And diue into the Sea to gather pearle, As faire as Iuno offred Priams ſonne, And you ſhall take your liberall choice of all. Her manhoode then is good I do beleeue. I find it ſo, right worthy gentlemen, And of that woorth your friendſhip I eſteeme, I leaue cenſure of your ſeuerall thoughts, But for requitall of your fauours paſt Reſts yet behinde, which when occaſion ſerues, I vow ſhal be remembred to the full, And for my fathers comming to this place, I do exſpect within this weeke at moſt. Valeria attend, I haue a louely loue, As bright as is the heauen criſtalline, As faire as is the milke white way of Ioue, As chaſte as Phoebe, in her ſummer ſports, As ſoft and tender as the azure dowlne, That circles Cithereas ſiluer Doues. Her doe I meane to make my louely Bride, And in her bed to breathe the ſweete content, That I, thou know'ſt, long time haue aimed at. Now Valeria, it reſts in thee to helpe To compaſſe this, that I might gaine my loue, Which eaſily thou maiſt performe at will, If that the merchant which thou told'ſt me of, Will (as he ſaide) goe to Alfonſoes houſe, And ſay he is my father, and therewithall Paſſe ouer certaine deedes of land to me, That I thereby may gaine my hearts deſire, And he is promiſed reward of me. He is, and Polidor ſhortly ſhalbe wed, And he meanes to tame his wife ere long. Sweetly reſolued, faire Em • lia, But would Philema ſay as much to me, If I ſhould aske a queſtion now of thee? What if the Duke of Ceſtus onely ſonne, Which came with me vnto your fathers houſe, Should ſeeke to get Philemas loue from me, And make thee Dutcheſſe of that ſtately towne, Would'ſt thou not then forſake me for his loue?
speeches.Emel:: Fie man, I know you will not die for loue, Ah Polider, thou need'ſt not to complaine, Eternall heauen ſooner be diſſolu'd, And all that pierceth Phoebus ſiluer eie, Before ſuch hap befall to Polidor. Should thou aſſay to ſcale the feare of Ioue, Mounting the ſuttle airie regions, Or be ſnatcht vp as erſt was Ganimede, Loue ſhould giue wings vnto my ſwift deſires, And prune my thoughts that I would follow thee, Or fall and periſh as did Icarus. And ſhould my loue, as earſt did Hercules, Attempt the burning vaults of hell, I would with pitteous lookes, and pleaſing words, As once did Orpheus with his harmony, And rauiſhing ſound of his mellodious Harpe, Intreate grimme Pluto, and of him obtaine That thou might'ſt goe, and ſafe returne againe. Should Polidor as Aehilles did, Onely imploy himſelfe to follow Armes, Like to the warlike Amazonian Queene, Pentheſelea Hectors paramour, Who foild the bloudy Pirrhus murd'rous Greeke, Ile thruſt my ſelfe amongſt the thickeſt throngs, And with my vtmoſt force aſſiſt my loue. That's better than a ſheepe.
speeches.Phil:: Why I am buying marchandiſe of him. I thanke you ſir, and would Philena might In any curteſie requite you ſo, As ſhe with willing heart could well beſtow. She is making of her ready, father, To goe to church, and if that he were come. Not for great Neptune, no not Ioue himſelfe, Will Philema leaue Aurelius loue, Could he enſtall me Empreſſe of the world, Or make me Queene and guidreſſe of the heauen, Yet would I not exchange my loue for his, Thy company is poore Phylemaes heauen, And without thee, heauen were hell to me. And ſhould my loue as erſt Leander did, Attempt to ſwimme the boyling H • lliſpont For Heros loue: no Towers of braſſe ſhould hold, But I would follow thee through thoſe raging flouds, With lockes diſ-ſheuered, and my breaſt all bare, With bended knees vpon Abidaes ſhore, I would with ſmokie ſighs and briniſh teares, Importune Neptune and the warry gods, To ſend a guard of ſiluer ſcaled Dolphins, With ſounding Tritons to be our conuoy, And to tranſport vs ſafe vnto the ſhore, Whilſt I would hang about thy louely necke, Redoubling kiſſe on kiſſe vpon thy cheekes, And with our paſtime ſtill the ſwelling waues.
speeches.Alfon:: How now daughters, is Ferando come? And where's your ſiſter that ſhe is not here? Go daughters, get you in, and bid your Siſter prouide her ſelfe againſt that we do come, And ſee you goe to church along with vs. I maruell that Ferando comes not away. Now Aurelius, what ſay you to this? What, haue you ſent to Ceſtus as you ſaid? To certifie your father of your loue, For I would gladly he would like of it, And if he be the man you tell to me, I gheſſe he is a Merchant of great wealth: And I haue ſeene him oft at Athens here, And for his ſake aſſure thee thou art welcome.
speeches.Eme:: Not yet father, I wonder he ſtaies ſo long.
speeches.Pol ▪: I warrant you hee'l not be long away.
speeches.Boy,: Wel ſirha, your faire words haue ſomething Alaid my choler: I am content for this once To put it vp, and be friends with thee, But ſoft, ſee where they come al from church, Belike they be married already.
Thei're euen aſwel matcht as I would wiſh. Great prince of Ceſtus, let a womans words Intreat a pardon in your Lordly breſt, Both for your princely ſon, and vs my Lord. How now Polidor? in a dumpe? what ſaiſt thou man?
speeches.Phile:: And yet I hardly thinke that he can tame her: For when he haz done, ſhe will do what ſhe liſt.
speeches.Manent: Seruingmen and eate vp all the meate.
I warrant you ſir, take you no care, Ile vſe my ſelfe ſo cunning in the cauſe, As you ſhall ſoone inioy your harts delight. Thanks Alfonſo, for thats your name I geſſe, I vnderſtand my ſon hath ſet his mind And bent his liking to your daughters loue, And for becauſe he is my only ſon, And I would gladly that he ſhould do well, I tel you ſir, I not miſlike his choiſe, If you agree to giue him your conſent, He ſhall haue liuing to maintaine his eſtate, Three hundred pounds a yeare, I will aſſure To him and to his heyres, and if they do ioyne, And knit themſelues in holy wedlocke band, A thouſand maſsie ingots of pure gold, And twiſe as many bars of ſiluer plate, I freely giue him, and in writing ſtraight I wil confirme what I haue ſaid in words. I humbly thanke your honor, good my Lord, And ere we part, before your honor here, Shal articles of ſuch content be drawne, As twixt our houſes and poſterities, Eternally this league of peace ſhall laſt Inuiolate and pure on either part. But Polidor, let my ſon and you take heed, That Ferando ſay not ere long as much to you. And now Alfonſo, more to ſhew my loue, If vnto Ceſtus you do ſend your ſhips, My ſelfe wil fraught them with Arabian ſilkes, Rich Affricke ſpices, Arras counter pointes, Muske, Casſia, ſweet ſmelling Ambergreece, Pearle, curtol, Chriſtal, jet, and iuory, To gratulate the fauors of my ſon, And friendly loue that you haue ſhewne to him. Why ſir, are you acquainted with my ſon?
Who's there? what Aurelius what's the matter That you ſtand ſo like a ſtranger at the doore? With al my heart, and if your honor pleaſe To walke along with vs vnto my houſe, We wil confirme theſe leagues of laſting loue.
speeches.Feran: Come hither ſirha: what haue you there?
A veluet cap ſir, and it pleaſe you.
speeches.Taylor: Why ſir, I made it as your man gaue me direc tion, You may read the note here
Item a faire round compaſſd cape. And a large truncke ſleeue. Item a looſe bodied gowne, I made it as the note bade me.
speeches.Tailor: Nay, nay, ne'r be ſo hot ſirha, for I feare you not. I thanke you ſir.
speeches.Feran:: Well ſir, what's your conceit of it? Tailer, come hither, for this time make it: Hence againe, and Ile content thee for thy paines. Come Kate, wee now will goe ſee thy fathers house, Euen in theſe honeſt meane abiliments, Our purſes ſhalbe rich, our garments plaine, To ſhrowd our bodies from the winter rage, And that's inough, what ſhould we care for more? Thy ſiſters, Kate, to morrow muſt be wed. And I haue promiſed them thou ſhould'ſt be there, The morning is well, vp, lets haſte away, It wil be nine aclocke ere we come there. I ſay tis but nine aclocke in the morning.
speeches.San:: I haue a deeper conceit in it than you Thinke for, take vp my miſtris gowne To his maiſters vſe.
speeches.Fera:: It ſhal be nine then ere you go to your fathers: Come backe againe, we will not goe to day: Nothing but croſſing me ſtil? Ile haue you ſay as I doe ere I goe.
Let Eole ſtorme: be mild and quiet thou, Let Neptune ſwel, be Aurelius calme and pleaſed, I care not, I, betide what may betide, Let fates and fortune do the worſt they can, I recke them not: they not diſcord with me, Whileſt that my loue and I do well agree. Let me intreat your grace vpon my knees, To pardon him and let my death diſcharge The heauy wrath your grace hath vowd againſt him. Thanks good my Lord, and I no longer liue, Then I obey and honor you in al. I for making a foole of her ſelfe and vs,
Thus al alone from Ceſtus am I come, And left my princely court and nobl • traine, To come to Athens, and in this diſguiſe, To ſee what courſe my ſon Aurelius takes. But ſtay, heres ſome it may be trauels thither, Good ſir can you direct me the way to Athens? Faire louely maide, yong and affable, More cleere of hew and far more beautifull Then pretious Sardonix or purple rockes, Of Amitheſts or gliſtering Hiaſinth, More amiable far then is the plain, Where gliſtering Cepherus in ſiluer boures, Gaſeth vpon the Giant Andromede, Sweet Kate entertaine this louely woman. I am glad ſir that you would be ſo franke Are you become the Duke of Ceſtus ſon, And reuels with my treaſure in the towne, Baſe villaine that thus diſhonereſt me? Her's no villaine: he will not know me now, But what ſay you? haue you forgot me too? Peace villaine, lay hands on th •• , And ſend them to priſon ſtraight. Ah trecherous boy that durſt preſume, To wed thy ſelfe without thy fathers leaue, I ſweare by faire Cintheas burning raies, By Merops head, and by ſeuen mouthed Nile, Had I but known ere thou hadſt wedded her, Were in thy breſt the worlds immortal ſoule, This Angry ſworde ſhould rip thy hateful cheſt, And hewd thee ſmaller then the Libian ſandes, Turne hence thy face, oh cruel impious boy. That damned villaine that hath deluded me, Whom I did ſend for guide vnto my ſon, Oh that my furious force could cleaue the earth, That I might muſter bands of helliſh feends, To racke his heart and teare his impious ſoule. The ceaſeleſſe turning of celeſtial orbes, Kindles not greater flames in flitting aire, Then paſsionate anguiſh of my raging breſt. Thankes good Alfonſo: but I came alone, And not as did beſeeme the Ceſtian Duke, Nor would I haue it knowne within the towne, That I was here, and thus, without my traine: But as I came alone, ſo wil I go, And leaue my ſon to ſolemniſe his feaſt, And ere't be long Ile come againe to you, And do him honor as beſeemes the ſon Of mighty Ierobel the Ceſtian Duke, Til when ile leaue you, farewel Aurelius.
speeches.Duke: I thinke the man is mad he cals me a woman. What is ſhe mad too? or is my ſhape transformd That both of them perſwade me I am a woman, But they are mad ſure, and therefore ile be gone, And leaue their companies for feare of harme, And vnto Athens haſte to ſeeke my ſon. With thy ſon? no truſt me, if he be thine, I pray you ſir, who am I? Aurelius ſtand vp, I pardon thee, I ſee that vertue wil haue enemies, And fortune wil be thwarting honor ſtil. And you faire virgin too, I am content To accept you for my daughter ſince tis don, And ſee you princely vſde in Ceſtus court.
My Lord, by heauens I ſweare vnto your grace, I knew none other but Valeria your man, Had bin the Duke of Ceſtus noble ſon, Nor did my daughter I dare ſware for her. I Ferando, the wager thou haſt won, And for to ſhew thee how I am pleaſd in this, A hundred pounds I freely giue thee more. Another dowry for another daughter, For ſhe is not the ſame ſhe was before.
speeches.Alfon: Let me giue thanks vnto your royall grace, For this great honor done to mee and mine, And if your grace wil walke vnto my houſe, I wil in humbleſt maner I can, ſhew The eternall ſeruice I do owe your grace.
Vpon mine honor, if I loſe Ile pay. I pray God your wife ſend you ſo good an an ſwere She may be buſie, yet ſhe ſaies ſheele come.
I promiſe thee Ferando I am afraid thou wilt loſe.
I promiſe thee Ferando I would haue ſworne, Thy wife would ne'r haue done ſo much for thee.
I ſure, and like a louing peece, your worthy To haue great praiſe for this attempt. You might haue kept it better then, Who bade you lay?
I ſay thou arte a ſhrew.
speeches.Tapſter: Now that the darkeſome night is ouerpaſt, And dawning day appeares in criſtall skie, Now muſt I haſte abroade: but ſoft, who's this? What Slie, O wondrous! hath he laine heere all night? Ile wake him, I thinke hee's ſtarued by this, But that his belly was ſo ſtufft with ale: What now Slie, awake for ſhame. A Lord with a murrin: come, art thou drun ken ſtill? Yea mary, but you had beſt get you home, For your wife will courſe you for dreaming heere to night. Nay tarry Slie, for Ile goe home with thee, And heare the reſt that thou haſt dreamt to night.
